title: arXiv Trending AI — Daily — 2026-11-13
global_caveat: arXiv has no official trending chart; this is an inferred, tentative evidence-ranked shortlist. Citation evidence for these very recent papers is limited, and this ordering does not indicate readership or downloads.

sections.title: AgentSSL: Can MLE Agents Leverage Unlabeled Data?
sections.abstract: The paper frames semi-supervised learning as agentic program search, reporting wins over human-engineered baselines in 8 of 12 settings while finding that choosing among generated programs can sharply reduce performance.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors introduce AgentSSL and ProgramSelectBench (16,977 programs) and report that agent-generated strategies beat the strongest human-engineered baseline in 8/12 settings, by up to 21.8%.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors report that on both ecology tasks their supervised AgentSL baseline matches AgentSSL, and identify unlabeled-data use and program selection as unresolved parts of the search problem.
sections.ranking_evidence: Cross-listed in AI and ML, marked NeurIPS 2026 in the arXiv record, and discussed by multiple technical write-ups; the official NeurIPS poster is a checkable venue signal.

sections.title: CapLite: Prompt-Injection Defense for Small Language Model Agents without Model-Written Security Artifacts
sections.abstract: CapLite derives write permissions from tool schemas and user-stated arguments rather than trusting an agent model to author its own security policy, and reports no successful attack across 13,935 attacked AgentDojo episodes.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors' CapLite design commits writes before reading tool results and permits them only when all consequential arguments were supplied by the user; their study reports zero successful attacks in the tested episodes.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors state that the evaluation uses only AgentDojo's four suites; CapLite's utility under attack is 21 points below the undefended agent, and the experiments use simulated environments rather than real users or accounts.
sections.ranking_evidence: Several separate technical summaries surfaced, alongside the unusually large reported attack evaluation; the external discussion is a visibility signal, not a readership measure.

sections.title: Unbundling Multimodal Vision Encoding
sections.abstract: In matched-compute experiments, the authors find that dedicated vision capacity matters more than a pretrained visual prior and can be placed inside early multimodal layers rather than in a separate pre-fusion encoder.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors isolate visual prior, dedicated vision parameters, and pre-fusion placement under common data and matched compute; they report comparable performance for early in-fusion modules and a conventional encoder.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors' controlled study uses dense backbones up to 6.4B parameters and 224×224 images; they leave sparse MoE models, higher-resolution training, richer data, and video/interleaved data for future work.
sections.ranking_evidence: The paper is cross-listed in vision and ML and received separate technical discussion from Sparse Notes and the Hugging Face paper page.

sections.title: LiveGeo: Benchmarking Geographic Agents in Continuously Evolving Worlds
sections.abstract: LiveGeo and its GeoWorld environment test whether agents can acquire current geographic evidence and revise decisions as locations, traffic, weather, and other world states change; the authors report substantial reliability drops in dynamic settings.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors release GeoWorld and a benchmark of 1,237 verifiable tasks across seven geographic task categories; in matched settings mean success falls 70.3% under task-only dynamics and 79.3% under shared dynamics relative to static settings.
sections.unique_caveat: The evaluation covers nine models, six cities, and 149 matched dynamic instances; the paper also finds that providing updates alone does not restore static-task performance.
sections.ranking_evidence: Independent technical coverage appeared at AI Understanding and CASRAI; the paper describes a benchmark and environment release. This supports inclusion but does not establish adoption.

sections.title: Ballad: Bandit-Based LLM Routing for Automated Heuristic Discovery
sections.abstract: Ballad adaptively routes heuristic-search steps among LLMs with non-stationary rewards, reporting that it can match or beat individual models on five combinatorial optimization problems while reducing API cost by up to 65.6% against always using the strongest model.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors combine online model selection, lineage-aware credit propagation, and discounting of stale outcomes to handle changing utility during heuristic evolution.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors' current formulation treats each LLM as a black-box generator with a fixed prompt, leaving model-specific prompting, mutation operators, and context representations untested.
sections.ranking_evidence: It has a NeurIPS 2026 poster listing and multiple technical write-ups; venue and external discussion rather than citation counts inform placement.

sections.title: Classical Energies Learn to Reason 1,000x Faster than Looped Models
sections.abstract: The authors train a Hopfield–Tank-style energy model, CRAM, for Sudoku and maze reasoning and report very fast puzzle training and substantially fewer inference FLOPs than looped-model baselines on those tasks.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors introduce CRAM and report at least 1,000× faster training than the compared looped models on Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Unique, plus at least 282× fewer inference FLOPs at matched Sudoku accuracy.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors explicitly caution that Sudoku and Maze are trivially solvable benchmarks and should not be used alone to assess the scalability of looped reasoning; results on these tasks do not establish general reasoning gains.
sections.ranking_evidence: The paper is cross-listed in AI and ML and has generated separate technical discussion and a public CRAM implementation.

sections.title: When Expert Disagreement Hurts: Prestige and Selectivity in LLM Decision Revision
sections.abstract: In a controlled revision audit, the authors find that expert-attributed disagreement can increase answer reversals without reliably improving accuracy, and that reversal counts alone can misrepresent whether a model corrected an error.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors propose a paired, two-pass audit and apply it to 1,989 evidence-grounded decisions across medicine, science, and law; they report accuracy losses of up to 16.1 points under expert disagreement.
sections.unique_caveat: The evidence comes from five models and controlled binary decisions in three professional domains; the paper does not establish how the measured effects generalize to open-ended tasks or other revision protocols.
sections.ranking_evidence: The arXiv record identifies NeurIPS 2026 acceptance; a matching NeurIPS poster, public code repository, and Hugging Face paper page corroborate the work and artifacts.

sections.title: Singularity-Bench: Can Agents Build Agents?
sections.abstract: Singularity-Bench measures agent-built systems across six AI-development tasks and reports that one tested agent setup matches or exceeds human-built baselines across all six, while the rest show uneven performance.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors introduce six end-to-end tasks and Breakwater, a Harbor extension that blocked every tested attack in their red-team evaluation; their strongest setup's Singularity-Index is 1.25.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors state that the task scale is smaller than that needed to measure true recursive self-improvement and that even the strongest agent leaves substantial headroom on raw task scores.
sections.ranking_evidence: The authors provide a detailed benchmark site and public repository, making its six tasks, baseline choices, and red-team setup checkable; this is a public-artifact signal rather than evidence of readership.

sections.title: Negative-Only Policy Optimization for One-Sided Verifiable Rewards
sections.abstract: NOPO trains from trusted verifier negatives while treating non-falsified outputs as unlabeled, and the authors report improved pass@k across code, logic, and math tasks when full correctness labels are unavailable.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors combine reference-relative negative suppression with a group-level support weight and report gains over baselines across unit-test, constraint-check, and LLM self-verifiers.
sections.unique_caveat: NOPO depends on trustworthy negative judgments; the authors note that weak negative-class recall reduces its supervision signal and that suppressing failures alone does not specify where probability mass should move.
sections.ranking_evidence: The arXiv record marks it as a NeurIPS 2026 Spotlight paper, and the authors provide a project page with the method, benchmark tables, and limitations.

sections.title: Goal Encoding in LLMs
sections.abstract: The authors use causal interventions in coding tasks to identify attention-head representations of upcoming sub-goals and propose that models sustain these representations by rereading task context rather than carrying recurrent state.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors report causal and transferable sub-goal encodings in sparse attention heads and test a non-recurrent goal-seeking account with targeted interventions.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors operationalize only pre-commitment, plasticity, and temporal persistence; they leave other goal attributes unresolved, and note that multi-token evaluation partly relies on an LLM judge.
sections.ranking_evidence: The paper is cross-listed in three core AI categories, has a project page with code and data, and has an OpenReview record plus external technical discussion.
